newsitem.title: UK: Welsh with thirst for change vote for Sunday pint.
newsitem.headline: Welsh with thirst for change vote for Sunday pint.

text.p: People in the last "dry" county in Wales voted by more than a 2-1 margin to overturn a 115-year-old law preventing them from drinking alcohol in pubs on Sundays.

Pubs in Gwynedd, a county about 250 miles (400 km) northwest of London and one of the last areas in Europe that was dry on Sundays, will be open throughout weekends for the first time since an 1881 act of the British parliament prevented the sale of alcohol on the Sabbath.

"It was an overwhelming victory. People will be celebrating with a pint of their favourite ale this Sunday," David Baird-Murray, chairman of the pressure group the Seven Day Opening Council, told Reuters after the result of Wednesday's vote.
The 65-year-old hotelier has been fighting the law since he founded the Seven Day Opening Council nearly four decades ago.

For 80 years after the 1881 act pubs throughout Wales were shut on Sunday. But in 1961 the Welsh were given the opportunity to vote, county by county, on whether to repeal the law in their local communities.
There have been six ballots since then and one by one counties across Wales have voted to go wet.
The Seven Day Opening Council estimates that pubs and hotels will see their takings increase by up to 25 percent.
"I was losing 12 months' trade every seven years because of the Sunday opening ban," said Portmadog pub landlord Robert Jones.
Baird-Murray said the Seven Day Opening Council would now cease to exist.
"Like Bob Dole, now I've nothing to do. The fight is finished," he said.
